newsitem.title: UK: Britain to hold new talks on N.Ireland parades.
newsitem.headline: Britain to hold new talks on N.Ireland parades.

text.p: Britain on Wednesday invited Northern Ireland's rival Protestants and Roman Catholics to talks aimed to defuse fears over volatile street parades during this summer's "marching season".

The discussions will be held on Friday at Hillsborough Castle, the official residence of Northern Ireland Secretary Mo Mowlam, south of Belfast, with the hostile groups accommodated in separate rooms, a British source said.

Mowlam and civil servants will liaise between Protestant march organisers and Catholic objectors from the town of Portadown, the main potential flashpoint, if they take up the talks offer, the source said.
"We are inviting the (Protestant) Armagh lodges and the (Catholic) Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition to Hillsborough Castle on Friday," a Northern Ireland Office spokesman said.
"It is the next logical step in pursuing the search for a local accommodation."

Mowlam, worried that traditional sectarian parades could again spill over into violence and worsen guerrilla conflict in the British-ruled province, has held a series of talks with rival groups in recent weeks.

If the Portadown groups accept, it would be the first time this year that they have met under the one roof to seek a compromise over a July 6 parade that many fear could spark a repeat of turmoil that erupted in 1996.
The Orange Order, the main Protestant marching fraternity, refuses direct talks with residents of the Garvaghy Road Catholic enclave, which is on the disputed route.

It says the group has links with Sinn Fein, the political wing of Irish Republican Army (IRA) guerrillas, who are fighting to end British rule in Northern Ireland and see the province united with the Irish Republic.
Catholics, who deny connections with republican hardliners, say that the annual procession by the staunchly pro-British Protestant "Orangemen" is offensive and anti-Irish.
Organisers say their parade is a simple celebration of religious faith and that the Catholics, who want an end to British rule, are intolerant.
Attempts to broker a deal in recent weeks have failed despite arms-length mediation by third parties.
Britain and its security chiefs are concerned that a flare-up in Portadown could ignite sectarian clashes elsewhere in the province and upset delicate moves to end the IRA's 28-year armed campaign.

Last year the region was embroiled in chaos for some two weeks when police banned the Orange march from entering the Portadown Catholic zone but relented after four days of province-wide trouble and allowed the marchers through.
